chapter: Book I, Chapter 7: The Restraint of the Senses (Indriyajaya)
text: The supreme aim of all political sciences is the restraint of the organs of sense (Indriyajaya). A ruler who abandons the six internal enemies—lust, anger, greed, vanity, arrogance, and foolhardiness—attains unshakeable mastery over his state. A king who cannot govern his own desires will swiftly perish, though he possess the wealth of the entire earth; but a sovereign who has subdued his senses and adheres to rigorous moral discipline secures the prosperity and loyalty of his subjects for generations.

chapter: Book I, Chapter 19: The King's Duty to the People
text: In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness; in their welfare his welfare. Whatever pleases himself he shall not consider as good, but whatever pleases his subjects he shall consider as the true good. Hence the sovereign shall ever be energetic and tireless in his duties; for the root of all economic success is persistent activity, and of disaster, negligence. If the ruler is awake and industrious, his officers and people will be equally diligent.

chapter: Book VI-VII: The Circle of States (Mandala Theory)
text: A contiguous bordering state is naturally an adversary, while the state situated beyond the adversary is naturally an ally. Strength alone is the cause of enduring peace; for between two equally formidable powers, alliances and treaties endure, but the weak are invariably dominated. A blazing fire unites with the wind to devour the forest, but the same wind snuffs out a frail spark. Therefore, a prudent ruler contracts peace with an equal or superior, crushes an irreconcilable foe, and never relies upon blind trust.

chapter: Chapter 2: The Testing of Friends and Adversity
text: Test a servant in the execution of orders, a relative in times of difficulty, a friend in adversity, and a companion in misfortune. He who stands by your side in disaster, famine, war, at the royal palace, and at the cremation ground is a genuine friend. Yet a wise person never places unconditional trust even in a friend; for should that friend become angry or suborned, he may weaponize your most intimate vulnerabilities.

A wise man perceives approaching danger from afar and prepares defenses before the crisis arrives. Protect your wealth as a fortress against sudden misfortune; but guard your self-respect and character above wealth, and protect your sovereign life above all else. It is far better to have no companion than a deceitful one, and far better to dwell in seclusion than to entrust your fate to an unruly ruler.

chapter: Book I, Chapter 4: The Rod of Justice (Danda)
text: That which guarantees the security of life, property, and moral order is the Rod of Justice (Danda). When administered with impartiality and wisdom, the rod fosters righteousness, enterprise, and social peace. But when wielded unjustly or with arbitrary wrath, it incites revolt even among sages. If punishment is withheld through cowardice, it invites the law of the fish (Matsya-nyaya), where the powerful ruthlessly swallow the weak.

Even from deadly poison, extract healing nectar; from an adversary, adopt useful virtues; and even from the mire, gather pure gold. The realist assesses human nature not by courteous words, but by concrete interests and deeds. Straight trees in the forest are felled first, and overly naive people are exploited first; therefore, let honest virtues always be armed with vigilant intellect and strategic realism.

chapter: Arthashastra Book I: Concerning Discipline & Training
text: Discipline is of two kinds: artificial and natural. Instruction and discipline impart qualifications only to a receptive mind, not to an unreceptive. Science imparts discipline to that mind which possesses such mental faculties as obedience, hearing, retention, deliberation, and discernment. Self-control is the basis of all knowledge. Hence the king shall overcome the six enemies: lust, anger, greed, vanity, haughtiness, and joy. A king of unrighteous character and vicious habits either falls a prey to the fury of his subjects or is conquered by enemies. Therefore, having mastered the senses, he shall develop his intellect by association with elders.

chapter: Arthashastra Book II: Treasury, Wealth & Revenue Administration
text: All state activities depend first of all on the treasury (kosha). Therefore the king shall look to the treasury first. A king with an exhausted treasury will swallow up the very people he is pledged to protect. Acquisition of wealth, maintenance of wealth, increase of acquired wealth, and dispensing of increased wealth on worthy objects constitute the fourfold economic duty. He shall look to the collection of revenue from mines, ports, forests, pastures, and trade routes. Wealth ensures righteousness and enjoyment. When wealth is lost, virtue and desire depart. Hence money is the bedrock of the state, but unrighteous extortion brings immediate ruin.

chapter: Arthashastra Book III: Law, Courts & Administration of Justice
text: The king who administers justice according to dharma, evidence, history, and statute law shall conquer the whole world as far as the four oceans. In disputes regarding boundaries, debts, deposits, and partnerships, the judges shall investigate without bias or wrath. Punishments must be proportioned to the offense: harsh punishment makes men terrified of the king, mild punishment invites contempt, while punishment properly meted out secures the allegiance and happiness of all citizens.

chapter: Arthashastra Book VI: The Source of Sovereign States & The Mandala
text: The King, the Minister, the Country, the Fort, the Treasury, the Army, and the Ally are the seven elements of sovereignty (saptanga). An ally who is loyal, hereditary, easily managed, and ready to assist in times of crisis is an ornament to the state. The king who is situated in the center and seeks conquest is the Vijigishu (the conqueror). The neighbor bordering his territory is naturally an enemy; the neighbor bordering the enemy is an ally. By understanding the twelve circles of kings (Mandala), the wise ruler preserves balance and avoids unprovoked destruction.

chapter: Arthashastra Book VII: The Sixfold Foreign Policy (Shadgunya)
text: Peace (Sandhi), War (Vigraha), Neutrality (Asana), Marching (Yana), Alliance (Samshraya), and Double-dealing (Dvaidhibhava) are the six forms of state policy. Whoever is inferior to another shall make peace with him; whoever is superior in power shall wage war; whoever thinks 'No enemy can hurt me, nor am I strong enough to destroy my enemy,' shall observe neutrality; whoever possesses an excess of strength shall march against the foe. Prudence, not hot-tempered wrath, determines the application of policy. The ruler who acts out of pique ruins his ministers and army alike.

chapter: Chanakya Niti: Wisdom on Human Suffering & Equanimity
text: Suffering in human life arises from unmastered desires, betrayal by unworthy associates, and the inevitable vicissitudes of fate and time. Just as a fire burns brighter when fed with dry fuel, so does suffering increase when the mind broods upon grievances. The wise man endures misfortune with steadfast patience (dhairya), knowing that prosperity and adversity alternate like the spokes of a moving wheel. Neither pride in victory nor despair in defeat belongs to the serene intellect.
